outcome: Piotr Bacik proved that the Skolem Problem is decidable for all algebraic linear recurrence sequences (LRS) of order at most 4, closing the remaining gap (general, non-real order-4 sequences) left after 1980s work had only established decidability for order ≤3 and real order-4 sequences; the general Skolem Problem (order ≥5, or unrestricted order) remains open, and a 2026 paper shows decidability would follow from a strengthened Cramér-type conjecture but this is conditional and unproven.
summary: The Skolem Problem asks whether it is decidable to determine if a constant-recursive (linear recurrence) sequence ever hits zero. As of the frozen revision (Jan 2024), decidability was known only for algebraic LRS of order ≤3 and for real algebraic LRS of order ≤4 (a 1980s result using Baker's theorem on linear forms in logarithms). Piotr Bacik's paper 'Completing the picture for the Skolem Problem on order-4 linear recurrence sequences' (arXiv:2409.01221, submitted 2 Sep 2024, revised through Dec 2025, accepted 21 Oct 2025 and published in TheoretiCS vol. 4 on 2 Dec 2025, DOI 10.46298/theoretics.25.28) extends decidability to *all* algebraic order-4 LRS, including the non-real case that had been open. This is a genuine case of the stated problem — order-4 LRS are a restriction of the general class of constant-recursive sequences — so it settles a case rather than the whole problem, hence 'partial' rather than 'resolved'. It has been peer-reviewed and journal-published (a strong form of expert digestion), and a March 2025 exposition by Yuri Bilu (arXiv:2501.16290) walks through the underlying results by Mignotte, Shorey, Tijdeman, Vereshchagin and Bacik, providing independent expert engagement. I also found follow-up work: Bacik, Ouaknine and Worrell, 'On the Complexity of the Skolem Problem at Low Orders' (arXiv:2507.11234, July 2025), and a July 2026 preprint 'Conjectural Decidability of the Skolem Problem' (arXiv:2607.15510) showing the general Skolem Problem would be decidable if a strengthening of Cramér's conjecture (about gaps between 'good' primes) holds, plus an unconditional result that large zeros of LRS have null density. That paper is explicitly conditional and not a proof of decidability. The order-5 case and the fully general problem remain open. I found no mention of AI, machine learning, LLMs, or automated theorem-proving/proof-assistant tools in any of these papers' methodology, acknowledgements, or abstracts (checked arXiv abstracts/HTML and the TheoretiCS publication page for 2409.01221, and the HTML of 2607.15510); the work is described throughout as traditional analytic/algebraic number theory (transcendental number theory, Diophantine analysis, Baker's theorem descendants). A broader search for AI angles (AlphaProof, AlphaEvolve, LLMs, neural networks) tied to the Skolem Problem or recurrence-sequence zero problems turned up nothing relevant — those systems' publicized mathematical work (IMO problems, AlphaEvolve's open-problem sweep) does not mention the Skolem Problem. I therefore classify ai_role as none.
competing_reading: One could argue the order-4 result is significant enough, and general enough in method, to be read as 'resolved' for a natural sub-statement ('the order-4 Skolem Problem') rather than merely 'partial' — but the Wikipedia bullet as given states the general problem for constant-recursive sequences of any order, so settling only order ≤4 is a case, not a full resolution, and 'partial' is the correct code under §3.1.
what_would_settle_it: An unconditional proof of decidability (or undecidability) for order-5 algebraic LRS, or a proof of the general case for all orders, would resolve the problem outright. Absent that, an unconditional (non-Cramér-dependent) argument establishing the same conclusion as arXiv:2607.15510 would meaningfully change the outlook.
